title: Reconstructing an organism’s cell divisions and histories from inherited molecular marks

concept.text: The innovation is a way to reconstruct an extensive cellular family tree: which cells share ancestors, how their lineages branched during development and adulthood, and, where timing can be calibrated, approximately when those branches arose. It would read inherited molecular marks in sampled cells and connect the inferred ancestry to measurements of their present molecular states. The intended capability spans multiple organs and life stages, with explicit estimates of error and uncertainty.

MethylTree illustrates the underlying approach using DNA methylation epimutations: changes in methylation that can carry information about shared cellular ancestry without requiring engineered lineage labels. Comparing these marks across cells can reveal clonal relationships. The central inference problem is separating ancestry-related similarities from methylation changes associated with cell type, differentiation and measurement noise. Connecting the resulting relationships to transcriptome measurements can then relate ancestry to cell state.

A cellular family tree provides a particular kind of history. Grouping cells by clonal origin does not necessarily recover every intervening division, and ancestry relationships alone do not supply calendar dates or a continuous record of past cell states. The proposed advance therefore combines lineage reconstruction with separately validated timing and state measurements; it does not assume that inherited marks preserve every event in a cell’s life.

significance.text: If sufficiently accurate and representative, this capability would make development and tissue maintenance accessible as retrospective histories linked to present cell states. Researchers could investigate how related cells diversify, how ancestral populations contribute to tissues, and how sampled disease-associated clones expand. MethylTree’s reported integration of methylation-derived clones with transcriptome-based state annotation, including reconstruction of a hematopoietic differentiation hierarchy, provides a limited experimental basis for that broader possibility.

The revolutionary prospect is the scale and integration of those histories: moving from selected clonal relationships toward a coherent account across tissues and life stages. With reliable timing, investigators could estimate when sampled disease-associated clones arose and compare their subsequent trajectories. These are conditional consequences of achieving adequate sampling, ancestry inference and temporal calibration, rather than capabilities established by the supplied benchmarks.

A family tree would remain an observational reconstruction. It would not, by itself, explain why a lineage adopted a particular fate, establish that a molecular change caused disease, or demonstrate that a treatment would work. Those conclusions would require additional evidence, including intervention experiments. Unsampled cells and extinct clones could also leave gaps, so even an extensive reconstruction would not automatically become a complete biography of the organism.

missing_breakthrough.text: The target capability is accurate reconstruction of extensive mammalian cellular ancestry across organs and life stages, with useful timing, calibrated uncertainty and links to measured cell states. The supplied MethylTree evidence establishes progress on selected populations and benchmarks, but does not demonstrate this broader capability. Because no freshness search record was supplied, it cannot establish whether the full target remained unmet on 1 November 2026.

The molecular information is incomplete and potentially ambiguous. The article describes single-cell genome-wide methylation measurements as typically covering approximately 5% of the genome. Sparse overlap between cells, measurement noise and differentiation-associated methylation changes make it difficult to identify which similarities reflect inheritance. Other lineage-tracing approaches also encounter rare or ambiguous inherited marks and limited temporal resolution. Resolving closely spaced divisions requires enough informative inherited differences to distinguish the branches concerned.

Readout and integration pose additional barriers. The article’s methods include cell lysis, so its description of tracing as noninvasive refers to avoiding engineered lineage labels rather than preserving each measured cell. Destructive single-cell readout complicates repeated observation of the same cells. Joint ancestry and state measurements help connect related cells to their measured identities, but do not directly reveal all of their earlier states.

Proposed engineering requirements include representative sampling across tissues, reliable inference despite missing observations, validation of division timing, and uncertainty estimates that remain informative outside favorable benchmarks. A high fraction of successfully reconstructed sampled cells would be insufficient if sampling systematically omitted important populations. Independent clone labels can validate shared origin, but may leave the intervening division sequence and dates unknown.

current_state.text: Chen, Fu, Chen, Li and Wang’s article, High-resolution, noninvasive single-cell lineage tracing in mice and humans based on DNA methylation epimutations, DOI 10.1038/s41592-024-02567-1, reports MethylTree results on selected datasets with known clonal or origin labels, together with lineage–cell-state analyses. The supplied research assigns a publication date of 16 January 2025. The reviewed artifact confirms the article’s identity but displays a publication-date placeholder, so that exact date is not independently confirmed by its content.

In the reported in vitro blood-differentiation benchmark, the article states that all 52 multicell LARRY clones were correctly identified in the similarity matrix. This supports successful recovery of known clonal groupings in that setting. The article’s Q metric evaluates grouping by clonal origin, and its evaluation excludes unlabeled cells and singleton clones. Consequently, a reported Q of 1 does not demonstrate recovery of every division, correct division dates, performance on all cells, or organism-wide completeness.

The supplied review also identifies joint lineage and state results: integrating methylation-derived clones with transcriptome-based cell-state annotations recapitulated a differentiation hierarchy in hematopoiesis. These findings support the feasibility of connecting ancestry information to measured state in selected populations. They do not establish a complete, multi-organ mammalian lifetime tree. The article’s suggestion that epimutations could in principle track lineages throughout life is a prospective rationale, rather than a demonstrated lifetime reconstruction.

The available assessment rests on the supplied review of a partial textual representation of the article. That review reaches beyond the abstract and introduction, but does not claim independent visual inspection of figures; pages 27–29 had no extracted text, and some pages remained uninspected. These limitations constrain interpretation of the reported results without showing that they are false. No bounded freshness search record was supplied, so the evidence cannot establish the field’s status through 1 November 2026.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: reconstruct cellular ancestry across development and adulthood in a complex mammalian model using a prespecified, representative sample spanning multiple organs. Define in advance the fraction of sampled cells to be covered, the closest divisions to be resolved, acceptable relationship and branch errors, timing accuracy, and uncertainty calibration. These would be proposed evaluation requirements, not established community standards; the supplied evidence does not justify inventing numerical acceptance thresholds.
completion_criteria.label: Multi-organ mammalian ancestry reconstruction meets prespecified evaluation requirements

completion_criteria.text: Proposed validation should use independently observable or engineered ground truth that matches each claim being tested. Clone labels can test whether descendants are grouped correctly, as in the supplied barcoded benchmarks. Stronger claims about individual divisions and their dates require ground truth that resolves those events. Validation should distinguish clone membership, branching relationships, division resolution and timing instead of treating one grouping score as evidence for all four.
completion_criteria.label: Claim-matched ground truth validates ancestry relationships and division timing

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reporting should quantify incorrect relationships, missed branches, unresolved divisions, sampling omissions and cells for which no reliable inference is possible. It should report sampled-cell coverage separately from estimated organism-wide coverage and explain how unobserved or extinct populations limit interpretation. Uncertainty estimates should be checked against known outcomes, including whether confidently reported relationships fail at the stated rate. Linking ancestry to cell-state measurements should include the uncertainty in both measurements.
completion_criteria.label: Reconstruction errors, coverage limits and calibrated uncertainty are reported

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility requirements include independent replication across animals, organs, developmental stages and relevant technical conditions, with sufficient data and methods to reproduce the reconstruction and error analysis. Practical assessment should document sampling burden, destructive readout, molecular coverage and the resources needed for reconstruction. Success would establish demonstrated breadth within the tested conditions; finite experiments would not establish literal universality across all cells, organisms or life histories.
completion_criteria.label: Independent replication reproduces reconstructions and error analyses across tested conditions

related_concepts.text: Roster comparison: GEN-01, A predictive, causal map of the genome’s regulatory code, concerns why regulatory sequences produce particular outcomes; GEN-08 reconstructs which cells descended from which ancestors. Combining the two could help investigate how regulatory programs unfold within lineages, but lineage association would not establish regulatory causation. GEN-11, Predicting genetic interactions across backgrounds and environments, similarly concerns the consequences of genetic combinations rather than ancestry reconstruction. Lineage information could contextualize those consequences without replacing interaction experiments or predictive models.

Roster comparison: GEN-05, General laws of environmentally induced, sequence-independent inheritance, overlaps through epigenetic inheritance. GEN-08 uses inherited marks as evidence of cellular descent; that use does not establish that an environmental exposure induced a mark, that the mark caused a phenotype, or that its inheritance follows a general law. Shared reliance on epigenetic information therefore does not make the two capabilities equivalent.

Roster comparison: GEN-02, Design and construct complex eukaryotic genomes to specification, and GEN-03, Precise, programmable replacement of large genomic regions in existing cells, concern constructing or rewriting genomes. Such engineering could support deliberately introduced lineage records or validation systems, but reconstructing ancestry from existing molecular marks is a distinct inference task. GEN-04, A retargetable delivery platform for genetic medicines across the body, concerns reaching selected cells with therapeutic payloads. Delivery could support engineered recording approaches, while broad delivery itself would neither recover a lineage tree nor be required by label-free methylation tracing.

Roster comparison: GEN-06, Transferable clonal seed reproduction across major crops, concerns reproducing a plant genotype through seeds; GEN-08 uses clonal relationships to infer cellular history. GEN-07, Predictably controllable inheritance in wild populations, concerns transmission and spread across reproducing populations. These operate at different levels from reconstructing somatic cell divisions within an organism, despite their shared vocabulary of inheritance and clones.

Roster comparison: GEN-09, An autonomous, evolvable expanded genetic alphabet, concerns an expanded molecular information system. GEN-08 instead interprets inherited information as a record of ancestry, without requiring an expanded alphabet. GEN-10, A testable reconstruction of the origin and fixation of the genetic code, concerns the historical emergence of the translation code. Its reconstructive aim is conceptually related, but its historical scale, evidence and mechanisms differ from those used to infer cell divisions.

Disciplinary synthesis: GEN-08 combines genetics and epigenetics with developmental biology, single-cell multiomics and computational phylogenetics. Inherited marks provide evidence for ancestry, state measurements describe sampled cells, and computational inference connects incomplete observations into possible histories. Each contribution addresses a different part of the problem; none alone establishes complete organism-scale reconstruction.

unresolved_issues: The exact publication date remains unconfirmed by the reviewed artifact; 16 January 2025 is supplied metadata rather than a date verified in its content.
No freshness search record establishes whether organism-scale, temporally calibrated reconstruction remained unmet on 1 November 2026.
Figures were not independently inspected in the supplied review, pages 27–29 lacked extracted text, and some pages remained uninspected.
Representative organism-wide sampling, suitable ground truth for individual divisions, and numerical acceptance thresholds remain to be specified for the proposed demonstration.
The extent to which unsampled or extinct lineages could be recovered, rather than remaining gaps in the reconstruction, is not resolved by the supplied evidence.

brief.title: A family tree of cells across a lifetime
possible: Researchers could trace how cells across your organs descended from shared ancestors, linking their family tree to what those cells are doing now. Inherited molecular marks would reveal branches in that tree, with approximate dates where timing can be reliably measured.
why: This would let researchers study how related cells take on different roles as bodies develop and maintain their tissues. They could also investigate when disease-associated cell families arose and how they expanded.

sources.who: Mengyang Chen, Ruijiang Fu, Yiqian Chen, Li Li and Shou-Wen Wang
sources.showed: Their method, MethylTree, used DNA methylation—chemical marks on DNA—to recover cell families, called clones, in selected tests. It also linked ancestry to cells’ present identities.
sources.quote: In native mouse blood, we identified ~250 clones of hematopoietic stem cells.
sources.cited_for: Inherited chemical marks can reveal shared ancestry and connect it to present cell identity.
sources.not_established: Correctly grouping relatives does not establish every division, its date or a family tree spanning an animal’s lifetime.

sources.who: Michael Scherer, Indranil Singh, Martina Maria Braun and collaborators
sources.showed: Their method, EPI-Clone, traced blood-cell families and their different roles in mice and humans. It revealed how expanding families contribute to ageing blood.
sources.quote: Applied to mouse and human haematopoiesis, we capture hundreds of clonal differentiation trajectories across tens of individuals and 230,358 single cells.
sources.cited_for: Blood-cell ancestry and present cell identity can be studied together at substantial scale.
sources.not_established: The work does not establish ancestry across organs, and the smallest cell families could not be individually identified.

sources.who: Sara Bizzotto, Yanmei Dou, Javier Ganz and collaborators
sources.showed: In a study of three people, inherited DNA changes revealed early embryonic branches and unequal contributions of ancestral cells to different organs.
sources.quote:
Using these variants as “endogenous barcodes” in single cells, 
we reconstructed early embryonic cell divisions.
sources.cited_for: Naturally occurring DNA changes can connect early human ancestry to cells across organs.
sources.not_established: Early developmental branches do not provide a continuous history through adulthood, and brain-cell sampling was uneven.

sources.who: Jisong An, Chang Hyun Nam, Ryul Kim and collaborators
sources.showed: They linked changes in DNA inside cells’ energy-producing structures to early ancestry. Damaging changes were held back from spreading to every DNA copy within a cell.
sources.quote:
The expansion of mtDNA-truncating 
mutations toward homoplasmy was substantially suppressed.
sources.cited_for: Early ancestry helps distinguish inherited DNA changes from changes acquired later in life.
sources.not_established: The work does not reconstruct all intervening divisions or connect a lifetime of ancestry to measured cell identities.

shown: Chen and colleagues recovered known cell families with MethylTree and linked ancestry to blood-cell identities. Scherer and colleagues extended this approach to large studies of ageing blood. Separate DNA-mutation studies have reconstructed early human branches across organs.
missing: A representative family tree spanning multiple mammalian organs, development and adulthood has yet to be demonstrated.
Individual divisions and their dates need validation against independently known histories.
Reliable estimates of errors, omitted populations and uncertainty are needed beyond selected tests.
Independent teams need to reproduce the full reconstruction and its error analysis across different biological and technical conditions.

milestones.label: Ancestry across organs meets agreed evaluation requirements
milestones.explanation: A mammalian reconstruction would have to span organs and life stages while meeting requirements set beforehand for coverage, branch accuracy, timing and uncertainty. This would demonstrate the intended breadth.

milestones.label: Independent histories confirm relationships and division dates
milestones.explanation: Independent observations or engineered labels would have to confirm each claimed relationship, division and date. This would distinguish finding cell families from recovering their detailed histories.

milestones.label: Measured errors and gaps match stated uncertainty
milestones.explanation: Results would have to quantify wrong relationships, missed branches, unresolved divisions and sampling gaps, with uncertainty checked against known outcomes. This would make ancestry and cell-state links interpretable.

milestones.label: Independent teams reproduce results across tested conditions
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to reproduce reconstructions and error analyses across animals, organs, life stages and technical conditions, while documenting practical demands. This would establish the demonstrated range of use.

uncertain: It remains unclear how much ancestry can be recovered when cell families were never sampled or have died out.
Chemical marks change with both ancestry and cell identity; separating those signals remains difficult.
Suitable reference histories and acceptable error thresholds for judging the full capability remain to be defined.

page.title: Mammalian cell lineage reconstruction from zygote to adulthood
page.definition: An ancestry tree connects sampled cells across a mammal’s organs to its fertilized egg using inherited DNA changes or methylation marks, chemical modifications of DNA. The reconstruction resolves ancestral divisions, estimates their timing and links sampled cells to measured molecular states, such as gene expression.

goal.need: A study of three human donors recovered early developmental branches using samples spanning 17 organs. A mouse experiment reconstructed 1,281,141 cells but covered only about 10% of one embryo at 13.5 days after fertilization. Connecting developmental ancestry to adult tissue maintenance requires histories that bridge these anatomical and temporal scales while retaining measurements of cell identity.

figures.caption: Coverage of the DNA Typewriter mouse reconstruction
figures.note: Published on 8 October 2026. Sampled-cell coverage does not establish recovery of every ancestral division.

statements.body: Allen Discovery Center for Cell Lineage Tracing
statements.quote: The goal is for each cell to be able to tell us its own individual history, including its lineage
statements.context: Michael Elowitz describing the centre’s goal in its Caltech announcement.

statements.quote: brings us closer to our dream of comprehensively mapping mammalian development
statements.context: Scientific director Jay Shendure discussing the DNA Typewriter mouse embryo experiment.

completion.title: A mammal’s multi-organ zygote-to-adult lineage reconstruction is independently validated and reproduced.
completion.criterion: A peer-reviewed study reconstructs ancestral divisions connecting sampled cells from multiple organs of one adult mammal to its zygote, links those cells to measured molecular states, and validates inferred relationships and branch dates against independently known histories. An independent team reproduces the combined capability. Unresolved divisions and unsampled populations remain explicit. No external numerical acceptance limits for coverage, topology error or dating error were found.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas; provisional operational test derived from the published organism-wide lineage and cell-history goals.
completion.basis: Searches of Allen programme documents, NIH/NIA funding calls, DREAM scoring rules and molecular-recording roadmaps found no completion test combining multi-organ mammalian ancestry, adulthood, branch timing and measured state. The provisional test joins those published objectives with independent validation and reproduction; published benchmark scores do not become acceptance thresholds.

milestones.title: Inherited molecular marks recover cell clones validated by independent lineage labels.
milestones.criterion: Recover groups descended from a common ancestor using inherited molecular marks, with assignments validated against separately acquired clonal labels. EPI-Clone, published on 21 May 2025, tested four recipient mice sampled 5 months after transplantation. Its adjusted Rand index against LARRY barcodes was 0.88 in the reported benchmark and 0.82 in a biological replicate. These scores concern clone membership, not recovery of intervening divisions.
milestones.set_by: Technology Atlas; the EPI-Clone benchmark and DREAM rules provide validation methods but no general clone-recovery pass threshold.

milestones.title: Cell-lineage measurements compare elderly and reproductively mature mammals.
milestones.criterion: Measure and compare cell lineages in elderly and reproductively mature adults, the minimum age comparison specified by the NIA funding call. EPI-Clone compared native blood formation in two 12-week-old mice and two 100-week-old mice. Expanded clones were larger in old mice, with a reported two-sided Wilcoxon test P = 0.012. This establishes an age comparison within blood formation rather than a continuous history of the same animal.
milestones.set_by: US National Institute on Aging, RFA-AG-11-001, Section I, critical points for applications; written for lineage tracing during mammalian ageing.
milestones.threshold_quote: Cell lineage tracing should be compared (at a minimum) between elderly and reproductively mature adults.

milestones.title: A mammalian embryonic lineage tree links ancestry, estimated branch times and measured cell states.
milestones.criterion: Reconstruct an embryonic ancestry tree from inherited molecular records, estimate branch times using a calibrated recording model and measure molecular states in its sampled cells. On 8 October 2026, Yu and colleagues reported a zygote-rooted tree of 1,281,141 transcriptionally profiled cells from one mouse embryo at 13.5 days. Dates were approximate; placement added limited branching information, and independent-animal confirmation remained outstanding.
milestones.set_by: Technology Atlas; Allen programme goals and the DNA Typewriter paper specify the components but no general acceptance threshold for their combination.

milestones.title: One adult mammal has a multi-organ lineage tree with branch-time estimates and measured cell states.
milestones.criterion: A single reconstruction connects sampled cells across an adult mammal’s organs to embryonic ancestors and assigns measured terminal states and branch-time estimates, before independent validation of the combined capability. Partial evidence comes from Bizzotto and colleagues, published on 19 March 2021: three donors aged 15, 17 and 42 years were studied, with targeted validation across 94 samples from 17 organs. Their trees recover early embryonic branches. No matching integrated zygote-to-adult demonstration was located.
milestones.set_by: Technology Atlas; searches of Allen programme goals, the NIA call and the molecular-recording roadmap found no externally specified integration test.

not_found: No external numerical acceptance limits were found for organism-wide sampling, branching accuracy, dating error or uncertainty calibration.
No independently reproduced reconstruction combining multi-organ mammalian ancestry through adulthood, validated branch dates and measured cell states was located.
The supplied MethylTree PDF exceeded the retrieval limit, and its Nature full text could not be opened.
The original Allen lineage-centre website and Synapse challenge page could not be opened; institutional announcements and the challenge’s GitHub scoring rules were accessible.

results.finding: In vitro blood cells from one mouse: 48 methylation-defined clones matched LARRY labels with an index of 0.98.
results.detail: The separately introduced LARRY barcodes provided clonal labels; the cells were cultured and differentiated in vitro.
results.quote:
We identified 
48 multi-cell methyl clones, which matched the observed LARRY 
clones (adjusted rank index of 0.98) (Fig. 3f,i,k).

results.finding: In one human embryo, inferred descendants of a four-cell-stage cell shared an inner cell mass fate.
results.detail: The study inferred early embryonic branches and linked them to cell fate, but did not estimate branch times using a calibrated recording model.
results.quote:
Inferred descendants 
from one four-cell-stage cell all adopted ICM fate, although another 
two putative four-cell-stage cells also contributed to ICM (Fig. 5h,i).

results.finding: In four recipient mice, EPI-Clone recovered expanded blood-cell clones with an adjusted Rand index of 0.88 against LARRY labels.
results.detail: The mice were sampled five months after transplantation. The score measures clone membership, not intervening divisions; small clones could not be individually assigned.

results.finding: In two young and two old mice, expanded blood-cell clones were larger in old mice (P = 0.012).
results.detail: The comparison used native haematopoiesis in 12-week-old and 100-week-old mice; it did not follow the same animals continuously.
results.quote:
Expanded clones in the old mice were individually also larger than in the young mice (Fig.
3c
; two-sided Wilcoxon test
P
= 0.012).

results.finding: In one human donor, 20 neurons resolved 82 somatic variants into early post-zygotic lineage clades.
results.detail: The study traced early clade contributions across 17 organs and linked some cortical cell types to lineage markers. It did not provide an integrated multi-organ tree with branch-time estimates and measured terminal states.
results.quote:
Single-cell WGS data of 20 single neurons (6, 7) from 1465 resolved 82/297 sSNVs into 
branching clades or clones, producing a lineage tree that spans early post-zygotic cell 
generations and traces the origin of each mutation back to the embryo (Fig. 2A, Fig. S2A, 
Tables S2, S5).

results.finding: Human cell lineages: 26 of 47 clones from a 93-year-old had an SVAF of approximately 1.0, versus none of 20 clones from a 37-year-old.
results.detail: The older donor’s clones were fibroblasts; the younger donor’s were colorectal clones. The comparison concerns mtDNA variants in separate individuals.
results.quote:
For example, in an older individual 
(DB8; 93 years old), 55% of clones (26 of 47) had an S VAF of ~1.0 by 1–3 
clone-specific PZsimple mutations (Fig. 4c). In contrast, in a young indi-
vidual (HC10; 37 years old), all clones exhibited an S VAF far below 1.0

results.finding: Human developmental phylogenies included 2,096 normal clones from 31 donors across three tissue types.
results.detail: The study reconstructed early embryonic phylogenies and examined expression in a subset of clones. The text does not report an integrated multi-organ tree for one adult with branch-time estimates and measured terminal states.
results.quote:
By leveraging WGSs derived from 2,096 healthy normal clones encom-
passing three different tissues, we elucidated the landscape of mtDNA 
mosaicism across single cells. Our system allowed the tracing of the 
embryonic origin of the mtDNA variants.

results.finding: MiTo recovered mitochondrial mutation-defined clones among 2,549 breast cancer cells, with ARI 0.94 against lentiviral labels.
results.detail: The cells came from a matched primary tumor and lung metastasis in one mouse. Two low-prevalence barcode clones were not detected as distinct mitochondrial clones; the result does not establish high-resolution recovery of intervening divisions.
results.quote: The final multi-modal dataset included 2 time-points, 2549 cells, 77 MT-SNVs, 13057 expressed genes, 33 MT- and 60 GBC-clones. Notably, MT and GBC clones showed very high concordance even across time-points (ARI = 0.94, Fig.

results.finding: Blood cell lineages in 3 young and 3 aged mice: 1,305 colony genomes underwent phylogenetic reconstruction.
results.detail: The mice were 3 and 30 months old. Somatic mutation-based phylogenies compared haematopoietic stem and progenitor lineages across age groups; these were separate animals.
results.quote:
We purified HSCs from three young (3 months) and three aged (30 months) healthy C57BL/6J female mice (Fig.
1a
and Extended Data Fig.
1a
), ages estimated to be the human lifespan equivalent of approximately 20 and 85–90 years, respectively (Supplementary Note
1
).

results.finding: Human blood-cell lineages: four elderly and four younger adults compared; expanded clones accounted for 32–61% of colonies in elderly donors.
results.detail: The study reconstructed blood stem and progenitor cell phylogenies. Each younger adult had at most one expanded clade; the comparison was cross-sectional.
results.quote: In each elderly individual, we found 12–18 independent clones established between birth and 40 years of age that each contributed between 1% and 34% of colonies sequenced, most in the 1–3% range.

results.finding: Mouse embryonic lineage trees linked cell states and estimated branch times for 1,447,839 donor cells across 16 embryos.
results.detail: Branch times were inferred from accumulated edits, with recording kinetics tested in vitro and in embryos. Trees traced donor stem-cell clones in chimeric embryos; they were not rooted at the zygote.
results.quote:
Here, we use PEtracer to continuously
install heritable genetic marks as development progresses, reconstructing
lineage trees that resolve ~75% of cell divisions across >1.4
million cells from 16 replicate embryos.

results.finding: One 6.5-week-old mouse: a multi-organ lineage tree reconstructed from 152 cells.
results.detail: The tree includes brain, kidney and liver cells, with inferred types for 47 of 71 brain cells. The paper places major splits in early development but does not report branch-time estimates; kidney and liver cell types were unassigned.
results.quote:
We applied RETrace2 to simultaneously pro ﬁle 152 single cells
from seven distinct tissue regions across the brain (anterior/posterior
cortex), kidney (left/right cortex), and liver (left/median/right lobes) of
a single 6.5-week-old female mouse (Fig.4a).
